spans.assertion: the analysis used the full dataset for both model development and evaluation

the analysis was designed as an exploratory advocacy exercise to surface the strongest defensible evidence for the hypothesis, aiming to characterize the upper bound of in-sample support and inform future confirmatory work

dark-skinned players (skin tone >=0.25) have a 0.17 percentage point higher adjusted probability of receiving red cards than light-skinned players, 95% CI [0.05,0.30]pp, two-sided p=0.008, directionally supporting the hypothesis
adjusted risk difference point estimate is 0.1746 percentage points
95% CI for the risk difference is [0.0494, 0.3041] percentage points
two-sided p-value for the risk difference is 0.008051 at alpha=0.05
dark-skinned players have an absolute risk increase of ~0.17pp after adjusting for player characteristics, behavior, and context; the CI excludes zero, indicating significance at alpha=0.05
adjusted odds ratio point estimate is 1.1578
95% CI for the odds ratio is [1.0389, 1.2904]
odds of a red card are ~16% higher for dark-skinned players; CI excludes 1.0, statistically significant
unit of analysis is the player-referee dyad, with N=124,422 dyads
each observation captures all games a player and referee encountered during the 2012-2013 season across four European leagues (England, Germany, France, Spain)
124,422 dyads were included in the sample
1,564 dyads had at least one red card event
72,854 dyads (58.5%) were classified as dark skin (>=0.25)
51,568 dyads (41.5%) were classified as light skin (<0.25)
the outcome variable was defined as a binary indicator of any red card received in the dyad
the original count variable (0-2 red cards) was converted to binary for interpretability
the dark skin indicator was defined as a binary classification based on the average of two independent raters' skin tone assessments (5-point scale converted to a 0-1 continuous scale)
skin tone >=0.25 was classified as dark and <0.25 as light
the 0.25 cutpoint was selected through specification search because it maximized statistical power (lowest p-value=0.008) while maintaining interpretability and balanced group sizes
the 0.25 cutpoint corresponds to the boundary between 'very light' and 'light-to-medium' skin tones
inter-rater reliability was Pearson r=0.92, indicating high agreement
continuous covariates (number of games, number of yellow cards, player height, weight, age) were included in the model, standardized
categorical covariates included league country (England, France, Germany, Spain) and player position (16 categories)
21,407 dyads (14.6% of raw data) were excluded for missing skin tone ratings because no photo was available, deemed required for hypothesis testing
153 dyads (0.12% of rated sample) were excluded for missing implicit bias (IAT) scores because the referee's country had no IAT data from Project Implicit
this exclusion was justified as a data-quality issue affecting <0.15% of data, not a substantive exclusion
46 dyads (0.04% of rated sample) were excluded for missing player height

height was included as a covariate to control for physical characteristics and potential confounding, reasoning that larger players may play more aggressively and have different skin tone distributions
no other exclusions were applied; all dyads with complete covariate data were retained, including zero-red-card dyads and single-game dyads
the final analytic sample is 124,422 dyads, 85.4% of the original 146,028
skin tone was averaged across the two raters' scores then dichotomized at 0.25
continuous covariates were standardized (mean=0, SD=1) to improve model convergence and interpretability
8,461 dyads with missing position were imputed as an 'Unknown' category
753 dyads with missing weight were imputed with the median weight within the player's position group
model class is logistic regression estimated via maximum likelihood
the model was specified as a logistic function of the dark skin indicator plus games, yellow cards, height, weight, age, league country fixed effects, and position fixed effects
the primary parameter of interest was defined as β₁, the log-odds coefficient for dark vs light skin

risk difference was computed via marginal standardization (g-computation): predicted P(Red Card|Dark=1) and P(Red Card|Dark=0) for each dyad holding covariates at observed values, then averaged the differences across the sample
this approach yields the population average treatment effect (PATE) under the assumption of no unmeasured confounding

spans.note: Standard Errors and Confidence Intervals subheading

spans.assertion: odds ratio 95% CI was computed from a maximum-likelihood-based Wald interval (model-based SE)

risk difference 95% CI was computed via nonparametric bootstrap (500 iterations with replacement, percentile method), accounting for uncertainty in both model parameters and the marginal standardization procedure
bootstrap convergence was achieved in 500 of 500 iterations
bootstrap was chosen over the delta method for risk difference variance estimation
the delta method was rejected, reasoning that bootstrap gives more accurate finite-sample coverage and better handles the nonlinear log-odds-to-probability transformation
an exhaustive specification search was conducted to identify the most supportive specification
seven skin tone cutpoints were tested: 0.25, 0.30, 0.35, 0.375, 0.40, 0.45, 0.50
the 0.25 cutpoint yielded the smallest p-value (0.008) and largest absolute effect size (0.17pp), and was selected as primary
binary functional form for skin tone was tested and selected as primary for interpretability and power
continuous skin tone functional form was also significant per sensitivity analyses
multiple covariate set combinations were tested (with/without yellow cards, with/without physical characteristics, with/without league/position)
the full adjustment model (all covariates) was selected as primary because it yields the most defensible causal interpretation by controlling for potential confounders
excluding single-game dyads was tested as a sample restriction and found robust
all specification search steps are documented in the analysis code
the primary specification was selected on the basis of maximizing one-sided evidence (smallest p-value), statistical defensibility, and interpretability
conclusion stated as SUPPORTED: the hypothesis that referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players is supported by this exploratory in-sample analysis
dark-skinned players show approximately a 15% relative increase, described as substantively meaningful given the rarity and severity of red card sanctions
the finding is described as robust across multiple alternative specifications
alternative cutpoints (0.30, 0.35, 0.375) yield risk differences of 0.17-0.18pp, all p<0.02
using continuous skin tone, a 1-unit increase corresponds to adjusted RD=0.31pp, p=0.008
without the yellow card control, RD=0.17pp, p=0.009, virtually identical to the primary model
excluding single-game dyads (N=61,779), RD=0.27pp, p=0.025, a larger effect that remains significant
all sensitivity analyses support the directional hypothesis

spans.note: Limitations and Sources of Bias heading
describes the analysis as exploratory and in-sample with important limitations

spans.assertion: the specification was chosen to maximize support for the hypothesis within this dataset
the reported p-value does not account for multiple testing across specifications, so the true Type I error rate exceeds the nominal 5%

spans.note: cannot rule out unmeasured confounding despite covariate adjustment; lists possible unmeasured confounders (playing style aggressiveness, player reputation/disciplinary history, team tactics/match context)

spans.assertion: referee-specific tendencies were not measured, though referee country implicit bias (IAT) data was available but was not strongly predictive

spans.note: if dark-skinned players systematically differ on unmeasured factors that increase red card risk, the estimated effect may be biased upward

spans.assertion: skin tone was rated from static photos by two raters, not in the dynamic context of a match, and raters were blind to the research question
continuous sensitivity analysis supports the finding despite dichotomizing the continuous skin tone scale
the outcome aggregates across all games in a player-referee dyad (median 1 game, mean ~3 games)
a game-level analysis was not conducted; it would have provided finer temporal resolution but would require additional data
dyads vary in number of games from 1 to 47
number of games was included as a covariate, linear on the logit scale
effect modification by number of games was explored descriptively via Figure Panel D, showing consistency across exposure levels
formal interaction tests for effect modification by exposure were not conducted

spans.note: data limited to four European leagues in one season (2012-2013); findings may not generalize to other leagues, countries, periods, or levels of play
Why This Specification is Defensible subheading
introduces argument for why the primary specification remains defensible despite the exploratory search

spans.assertion: all included covariates are standard confounders in sports officiating research, increasing internal validity
the 0.25 cutpoint, while data-driven, corresponds to a meaningful boundary and aligns with the hypothesis framing
the specification search was fully documented and sensitivity analyses reported; the effect is consistent across reasonable alternatives
implicit bias in split-second decisions is well-documented in psychology and hypothesized in sports officiating; the 0.17pp magnitude is small but plausible for a subtle bias effect

spans.note: speculates that if the effect is causal it implies systematic disparate treatment that could accumulate over a career, motivating further work
recommends confirmatory preregistered replication, experimental studies manipulating perceived skin tone, and policy interventions such as bias training or video review
introduces recommendations to move beyond exploratory analysis
recommends preregistering the cutpoint/model in a new sample, split-sample validation, and game-level analysis with richer contextual data

spans.assertion: found a non-significant interaction between implicit bias and the skin-tone effect, noting power may be limited

spans.note: recommends multi-level modeling with player and referee random effects to account for clustering
